newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Enviroment council agrees CO2 deal.
newsitem.headline: Enviroment council agrees CO2 deal.

text.p: Environment ministers reached a deal on Monday to go to international climate talks later this year committed to cutting greenhouse gases by 15 percent of 1990 levels in 2010, as long as other rich countries follow suit.

Informal talks late on Sunday and hours of closed-door talks on Monday produced a deal confirming the 15 percent negotiating target for international talks while trimming the share out of emissions cuts proposed by the Dutch ahead of the meeting.
Talks on climate overshadowed all else at the meeting, which the Dutch cut to one day from the two days originally scheduled.
Ministers also discussed suggested improvements to implementation of Community environment law following on from the Commission's communication on the issue, promising to come back to it in June.
Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard played down reporters' suggestions at a late Monday news conference that the text was a much watered-down version of Commission ideas.

"I think it would be very good if we could make progress on access to justice, that's what I stressed today. We will have to wait for the European Parliament (to take a decision). I think a number of the aspects in the communication are certainly vaguely worded but we have not finished discussing this yet," she said.
Ministers also discussed over lunch the latest developments in the leg-hold trap debate and Regulation 3254/91.

Gone were the strong words of last December when ministers called for tougher trap norms to be negotiated between the EU, Canada, Russia and the United States while at the same time ordering the Commission to prepare fall-back legal texts for a fur import ban to begin at the end of March.

Ministers will return to the issue in June to review any progress made in talks between the Commission and the other negotiating parties, with the option of rejecting any compromise text by unanimity if they are not happy.
Discussions then moved to the Commission's Auto/Oil proposals, COM(96)248, which ministers first discussed in an open session on October 15 in Luxembourg.
Time spent on climate talks meant discussions on this were severely curtailed, leaving member states in more or less the same positions after the Council as they had been before.

De Boer postponed, until after a ministerial dinner involving the Council and environment ministers from central and east European countries (CEECs), her efforts to forge a political agreement for a common position on the decision for a Community action programme promoting environmental non-governmental organisations.

The proposal for NGO co-financing, intended to run from January 1998 to the end of 2001, would earmark 10.6 million Ecus to be used in funding up to half of a qualifying organisation's budgeted activity.

Also delayed until after the dinner were planned discussions of the Commission's communication on environmental agreements, a Commission presentation of its proposal for a directive intended to limit industrial emissions of volatile organic compounds, COM(96)538 and of its recent proposal for a framework directive on water policy (see BC-ENVIRONMENT-WATER, moved on Wednesday).

Before dinner, ministers held a working session their counterparts from the central and eastern European countries (CEECs), namely Estonia, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia.
Talks centred on CEECs' efforts to cut their consumption of energy while maintaining economic growth targets, an issue which de Boer said most of the countries had agreed was possible.
The issue of joint implementation of climate gas targets also came up, she said.

"We have identified possibilities whereby you can use this instrument. Countries who do not have the possibilities to achieve energy savings, those countries could avail themselves of joint implementation in eastern Europe but we must remember that there are two binding conditions," she said.

The idea of joint implementation is that countries looking for cuts in their own emissions agree reduction strategies with poorer countries for equivalent cuts to be acheived there, often De Boer said the conditions should include that there be no back sliding by either party on their pledged greenhouse gas targets and robust enforcement and monitoring procedures for any joint implementation agreements.
